content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Tutorial: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) and Traffic Sniffing (Wireshark, Ettercap)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"This technical tutorial explores the mechanics of Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks and network traffic sniffing within a controlled, ethical hacking environment. Understanding these concepts is vital for securing modern network infrastructures against unauthorized eavesdropping and data tampering."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"Prerequisites and Setup"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"A dedicated lab environment running Kali Linux (attacker) and a vulnerable target machine (e.g., Windows 10 or an older Linux distro)."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Ettercap installed on the attacker machine for ARP spoofing."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Wireshark for packet analysis and traffic inspection."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Explicit authorization to test the targeted network segment."},{"order":8,"type":"heading","text":"Step 1: Enabling IP Forwarding"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before launching a MitM attack, the attacker system must be configured to forward packets it receives instead of dropping them. If IP forwarding is disabled, the target machine will lose internet connectivity immediately upon ARP poisoning, alerting the user."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1"},{"order":11,"type":"heading","text":"Step 2: Performing ARP Spoofing with Ettercap"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"ARP spoofing (or ARP cache poisoning) involves sending forged ARP messages over a local area network. This associates the attacker's MAC address with the IP address of a legitimate node, such as the default gateway."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"sudo ettercap -G"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Within the Ettercap graphical interface, perform the following actions: 1. Sniff -> Unified sniffing (select your network interface). 2. Hosts -> Scan for hosts. 3. Hosts -> Hosts list to view discovered devices. 4. Add the target IP to Target 1 and the gateway IP to Target 2. 5. Mitm -> ARP poisoning -> Check 'Sniff remote connections'."},{"order":15,"type":"heading","text":"Step 3: Traffic Sniffing and Analysis with Wireshark"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"With the MitM position established, all traffic between the target and the gateway flows through the attacker's machine. Open Wireshark to capture and inspect this traffic."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"sudo wireshark"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Select your active network interface and apply display filters to isolate relevant data. For example, to inspect HTTP cleartext credentials, use the following filter:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"http.request.method == \"POST\""},{"order":20,"type":"heading","text":"Mitigation and Defense Strategies"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use encrypted protocols (HTTPS, SSH, TLS) to ensure data confidentiality and integrity, preventing cleartext credential harvesting."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Implement Static ARP Entries on critical servers and network gateways to prevent unauthorized mapping changes."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Deploy Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches to validate ARP packets against trusted binding databases."}]
